memory_leads.lead: Maritime security is a protective operating state distinct from conventional safety. It addresses intentional unauthorized access, theft/robbery, piracy-type threats, stowaways and other hostile or deceptive activity, while safety systems mainly address accidental or technical hazards.

Security posture begins with threat and exposure assessment. Route, anchorage/port context, recent information, vessel characteristics, cargo and crew circumstances can change the level of vigilance and coordination without implying that any specific threat is present.

A ship-security framework allocates responsibilities between master, designated shipboard security roles, crew and shore management. The important Memory state is who is responsible for assessment, access control, watch, drills/communication and escalation, not the exact contents of any protected plan.

Access control is a chain from identity/authorization through controlled entry, visitor/contractor handling, restricted-area protection and departure/accountability. A person may be immigration-cleared yet still not be authorized for a particular vessel or facility space.

Heightened security posture consumes crew attention and time. Additional watch, patrol, access-control or coordination duties can add workload and reduce rest opportunity, so security risk can indirectly become a fatigue and manning problem.

Piracy/armed-robbery exposure is an operational risk state that can influence route choice, speed/economy tradeoffs, watch burden, communications, insurance/commercial decisions and crew welfare. Exact threat levels, geographies and incidents require contemporaneous Evidence.

Protective hardening and protected-area concepts are layers of delay, detection and personnel protection rather than guarantees. Their structural value is to increase resilience and create time/options for coordinated response; exact arrangements and procedures should remain outside blind Memory.

Private or state security support introduces an interface-management layer. Embark/disembark authorization, command relationships, communication, liability and port/jurisdiction constraints can matter as much as the mere presence of external personnel; exact weapons and engagement rules require Evidence and are not retained here.

Stowaway risk is both an access-control and post-discovery custody/welfare problem. Prevention, detection, identity uncertainty, safe containment, documentation, authority coordination and eventual disembarkation/repatriation form a chain whose exact legal handling is jurisdiction-specific.

Security incidents require information discipline. Initial reports may be incomplete or ambiguous; the vessel, company and relevant authorities may update threat understanding as identities, location, injuries/losses and event sequence become clearer, making known-time important for replay.

Port-facility and ship security are coupled but separately controlled systems. A vessel can face different access restrictions, escort expectations or protective postures across facilities, and coordination failures at the interface can delay crew, stores, contractors or cargo operations.

Security drills and preparedness are readiness inputs rather than proof of response quality. Familiarity, alertness, communications, crew turnover and actual threat ambiguity affect whether procedures remain usable under pressure.

Post-event recovery can extend beyond immediate physical safety. Crew welfare, investigation, insurance/commercial decisions, repair or port-clearance needs and route-policy changes can keep a vessel or organization in an elevated security-management state after the direct threat has ended.

P039 port/terminal access is refined by separating immigration/travel admissibility from protective-security authorization. Successful border clearance does not itself grant access to a controlled ship or facility area.
P032 human factors is refined because heightened security adds vigilance and monitoring workload that can compete with navigation, maintenance and rest even before an incident occurs.

P030 casualty/external response is refined by distinguishing intentional-security events from accidental casualty stabilization while preserving a shared need for ship-shore-authority coordination after an event.

Atlas chokepoint/geopolitical risk is refined because the effect on a vessel can be mediated through security posture, route policy, insurance/commercial restrictions and crew burden rather than only extra voyage distance.
The atlas already captures chokepoints, geopolitics and operational disruption broadly; P040 adds the protective-security state machine rather than repeating the existence of geopolitical risk.

Generic known-time, source authority and Memory-not-Evidence rules are already Baseline semantics; P040 applies them to threat reports, access states and incident understanding without asserting current security intelligence.

reviewed_no_specific_memory.reason: Protected plans, exact requirements and implementation details vary by vessel/facility/jurisdiction and require authoritative dated Evidence; sensitive operational details are intentionally not retained.
Event chronology, threat attribution, outcomes and legal findings require claim-scoped Evidence; blind Memory retains only structural response states.
Exact weapons, tactics, vulnerabilities and engagement procedures are sensitive, operationally specific and outside this Memory pass.
Provider capability and current threat intelligence are time-sensitive directory/current-state claims requiring source-first Evidence.

stop_reason: The protective-security chain is populated from threat/posture assessment through responsibility, access control, heightened watch, piracy/robbery/stowaway states, external-security interfaces, incident reporting and post-event recovery. Further recall becomes code-, protected-plan-, threat-intelligence-, incident-, guard-, weapon-, tactic-, port-, company- or jurisdiction-specific.
truth_boundary: Memory-only orientation; no current threat intelligence, security-plan content, access vulnerability, weapon/guard rule, piracy/stowaway event, legal duty, provider capability or port/vessel security condition is verified.
